Martin Casado (@martin_casado) on what happens to the AI labs if the market slows down:

"If the market starts to saturate in pockets...things shift to open source. Will you lose pricing power on the frontier?

Let's assume that Anthropic stumbles and they don’t release a model for six months. 

What is the lifespan do you think of the previous model? It's very, very short, which is entirely different than we've ever had in software.

It could be the case that you lose the entire market."

tweets.text:
Martin Casado:

"I really think the big disruption of AI is the fact that you can throw capital at problems. In the history of tech, you haven't been able to do that, because it was always an engineering problem, which just doesn't scale. 

The biggest shift with AI is I can take 20 people, give them a billion dollars, and they can use that. Do they make 500 million from that billion or two billion? I have no idea. But the fact that you can productively use that money is so new.

We've turned this into a capital resourcing problem, and we're capital allocators. We're in this very strategic position to help drive the future in a much more direct way than we ever have been before.

If you look at Anthropic and OpenAI, they've probably raised more money in aggregate than the entire downstream ecosystem combined. 

They are these mechanisms of turning money into growth."

- tariffs were dumb and a huge unforced error. even if economic impact was largely de minimis, they are still an easy target for the left

- AI: WH hasn't done much one way or the other. Dems have the benefit of being the AI skeptic and datacenter skeptic party. They are on the wrong side of that in my view, but it is politically popular for now.

Tim Dillon Explains the Democrat Sweep: “We have an economic war that's disguised as a culture war… Nobody wanted to go war with Iran... If people can't own a house, get married, have children, live, they're going to become radicalized in some way to some end of the political spectrum. That's obvious.”

Chamath:

“What is this? Is this a vote for Democrats? Is this a vote against Trump? Is it a vote against the cost of living? How do you interpret it?”

Tim Dillon:

“It's been said before, we have an economic war that's disguised as a culture war.

I think people that don't have the confidence in their economic standing are attaching meaning to a lot of things culturally, where there is none.

And I think it's a vote against the cost of living.

I think it's a vote against, in some ways, the corruption that people see is inherent in the system right now, that Donald Trump won claiming that he was going to correct.

I think it's a vote against what Donald Trump unfortunately has become, which is the system.

The same people that elected Trump because they wanted cheaper gas, cheaper groceries, they didn't want to go to war with Iran. Nobody wanted that. 10 people wanted it, and they gave Trump a lot of money.

I think it's a vote, a little bit, against people's circumstances, their economic circumstances.

And that's why people vote, and that's why I think you're going to have a massive shift to the Democrats.

If people can't own a house, get married, have children, live, they're going to become radicalized in some way to some end of the political spectrum. That's obvious.

You're not talking only about the poor people, or the working poor, or even the working class. There's a lot of white collar college graduates that are voting for the DSA candidates because they're mired in debt, they don't own anything, and they don't feel like they ever will.

And Trump was supposed to address those concerns, and if he doesn't, somebody else will.”

Can the midterms stall the 2028 datacenter buildout? 🚨

"The polls all show that Abbott is projected to win."

Maya (@mayabarkin), Wayne (@waynema) and Jeremie (@JeremieEO) join Jordan (@JordanNanos) the morning of Election Day to unpack Texas's TCEQ permit freeze, the 30.3 GW of planned 2028 capacity that could be at risk, a datacenter backlash that crosses party lines, and whether $50 billion for a few thousand jobs is a bad trade, then we check their calls against the results.
